qs.q: What is the primary cellular defect defining bone marrow failure or aplastic anaemia?
o: Failure of bone marrow cells to produce normal mature cells
Malignant clonal expansion of myeloid progenitor blood cells
Destruction of circulating red blood cells by autoantibodies
Ineffective erythropoiesis due to vitamin B12 deficiency
qs.e: Bone marrow failure is specifically defined as the failure of bone marrow B cells to produce the normal number of mature cells resulting in peripheral blood cytopenias. Clonal expansion refers to conditions like myeloproliferative disorders rather than pure aplastic anaemia.

qs.q: What finding is expected on a bone marrow trephine biopsy in a patient with aplastic anaemia?
o: Hypercellular marrow featuring complete erythroid hyperplasia
Reduced haemopoietic tissue with increased fat spaces
Packed marrow completely replaced by blasts and leukemic cells
Fibrotic tissue replacement with marked bone osteosclerosis
qs.e: Bone marrow trephine biopsy in bone marrow failure shows reduced haemopoietic tissue with increased fat spaces and stroma. Hypercellularity is characteristic of marrow infiltrations or myeloproliferative disorders rather than primary aplastic anaemia.

qs.q: A 68-year-old woman is found to have 2.1 g/dL of monoclonal IgG in her serum on a routine check. She has no bone pain, no anaemia, no Bence Jones proteinuria, and bone marrow shows 8% plasma cells. She is asymptomatic. What is the risk of this condition progressing to symptomatic myeloma?
o: A. It will never progress as plasma cells are below 10%
B. It progresses at approximately 1% per year and contains the same chromosomal translocations as myeloma
C. It progresses rapidly within 1–2 years in all patients
D. It only progresses if the M protein exceeds 3 g/dL
qs.e: This is MGUS — the most common plasma cell proliferation, found in 1–3% of healthy persons over 50. Despite its name, MGUS is a precursor lesion that progresses to symptomatic plasma cell tumour at approximately 1% per year. The clonal plasma cells in MGUS already contain the same chromosomal translocations as full-blown myeloma. Diagnosis of MGUS requires less than 3 g/dL monoclonal protein and no Bence Jones protei

qs.q: A 65-year-old man presents with massive splenomegaly and anaemia. Peripheral blood smear shows teardrop cells, nucleated red cells, and immature myeloid cells. Bone marrow trephine is hypocellular and fibrotic. Which of the following BEST explains the origin of the marrow fibrosis?
o: A. Neoplastic fibroblasts proliferating as part of the malignant clone
B. IL-6 secreted by myeloma cells stimulating collagen deposition
C. BCR-ABL signalling directly activating fibroblast growth factor receptors
D. TGF-β and PDGF released from neoplastic megakaryocytes stimulating non-neoplastic fibroblasts
qs.e: This is primary myelofibrosis — teardrop cells, leukoerythroblastosis, and fibrotic marrow. A critical concept is that the fibroblasts are NOT part of the neoplastic clone. The fibrosis is secondary — stimulated by PDGF and TGF-β released from neoplastic megakaryocytes. BCR-ABL is the driver in CML, not primary myelofibrosis. IL-6 drives myeloma cell proliferation and bone resorption, not marrow fibrosis.

qs.q: In iron-deficiency anaemia, which laboratory marker most directly reflects depleted iron stores and is typically decreased?
qs.e: Ferritin reflects iron stores and drops early; TIBC rises in IDA.

qs.q: Morphological classification of anaemias is based on ---
qs.e: Microcytic/normocytic/macrocytic classification is based on MCV (cell size).

qs.q: A patient presents with recurrent infections, petechiae, and anaemia. A bone marrow biopsy shows reduced cellularity. What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.e: The triad of infections (low WBC), petechiae (low platelets), and anaemia (low RBC) reflects pancytopenia; combined with a hypocellular marrow, this is diagnostic of aplastic anaemia — failure of the marrow to produce blood cells of all lineages.

faq.a: Dietary iron is low, malaria and helminths cause chronic blood loss, and iron supplements are often unavailable.
faq.q: Why is iron deficiency still the leading cause of anaemia in East Africa?

faq.a: No; early iron deficiency may be normocytic, so ferritin or response to iron trial is needed.
faq.q: Can a normal MCV rule out iron deficiency?

faq.a: In severe anaemia (<5 g/dL in children, <6 g/dL with cardiac disease) or when the patient is unstable (tachycardia, hypotension, altered consciousness).

exam: A 28‑year‑old woman with heavy menstrual bleeding presents with Hb 9 g/dL. What investigations would you order and why? — Full blood count, MCV, ferritin; to differentiate iron deficiency from other causes and guide therapy.
A child with malaria has Hb 5.5 g/dL but is alert. What is your next step? — Give prompt antimalarial therapy, arrange blood transfusion if signs of cardiac compromise develop.

You see a patient with pallor, splenomegaly and a reticulocyte count of 8 %. What is the most likely category and next test? — Haemolytic anaemia; order peripheral smear for sickle cells or malaria parasites.
A pregnant woman at 32 weeks has Hb 10 g/dL. How do you manage her? — Assess iron status, start oral iron if deficient, monitor for progression; transfuse only if severe or symptomatic.

Why is folic acid preferred over vitamin B12 in macrocytic anaemia in a malaria‑endemic area? — Folate deficiency is common due to poor diet and antimalarial drugs; B12 deficiency is rare and requires different work‑up.
A patient on zidovudine develops anaemia. What is the mechanism and alternative? — Zidovudine causes marrow suppression; switch to a non‑myelotoxic ART regimen if possible.

Explain why a normal ferritin may be misleading in chronic infection. — Ferritin is an acute‑phase reactant and can be elevated despite iron deficiency; consider transferrin saturation or trial of iron.
What bedside sign helps differentiate anaemia from hypovolaemia? — Presence of a rapid, regular pulse with warm extremities suggests anaemia; cold clammy skin points to hypovolaemia.
ai.title: Anaemia
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Anaemia is a reduction in haemoglobin or red cell mass causing inadequate oxygen delivery. It is common in low‑resource settings and has many reversible and life‑threatening causes.

b: Assess impact: fatigue, dyspnoea, tachycardia, pallor.
Identify whether the problem is reduced production, increased loss, or increased destruction.
sections.p: Anaemia is defined by WHO thresholds: <13 g/dL in men, <12 g/dL in non‑pregnant women, <11 g/dL in pregnant women. Severity is mild (10‑11 g/dL), moderate (7‑9.9 g/dL) or severe (<7 g/dL).

b: Microcytic, hypochromic → iron, thalassaemia, chronic disease.
Normocytic, normochromic → acute blood loss, chronic kidney disease, haemolysis.
Macrocytic → folate, vitamin B12, marrow failure, drugs.
sections.p: Classify anaemia by red cell indices and reticulocyte count, then apply a cause‑based algorithm. In low‑resource settings, common aetiologies are nutritional deficiency, chronic infection, haemoglobinopathies and drug‑induced marrow suppression.

b: Look for signs of decompensation: tachycardia >120 bpm, hypotension, altered mental status.
Consider transfusion when haemoglobin <5 g/dL in children or <6 g/dL with cardiac disease.
sections.p: Anaemia worsens outcomes in malaria, HIV, TB and pregnancy. Severe anaemia (<7 g/dL) can precipitate cardiac failure, cerebral hypoxia and death, especially in children and pregnant women.

t.b: Confirms anaemia, gives MCV and reticulocyte count; guides classification.
Detects malaria parasites, sickle cells, schistocytes; essential when microscopy is available.
Distinguish iron deficiency from anaemia of chronic disease; if unavailable, use transferrin saturation or response to iron trial.
High count → haemolysis or blood loss; low count → production problem.
Identifies chronic kidney disease as a cause; guides use of erythropoietin if available.
Detects HIV‑related marrow suppression or opportunistic infections.

b: Ask about diet, menstrual losses, deworming, malaria episodes, HIV/TB status, drug history.
Examine for pallor (conjunctiva, nail beds), jaundice, splenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, cardiac murmurs.
sections.p: Examiners expect you to integrate history, bedside findings and limited investigations to reach a working diagnosis and immediate management plan.

b: Assuming all microcytic anaemia is iron deficiency without checking for thalassaemia or chronic disease.
Missing severe anaemia that needs urgent transfusion because the patient appears “well‑looking”.
sections.p: Students often jump to a diagnosis without confirming the type of anaemia or overlook reversible causes that are treatable with simple measures.

whenToSeekHelp: Chest pain or syncope suggesting cardiac ischemia
